To understand the structural violation loss functions reused during relaxation analysis, see [FAPE and Structural Losses](10-fape-and-structural-losses). For the CLI command covering relaxation alongside prediction and evaluation, see [CLI Command Reference](21-cli-command-reference).

# Distributed Training Infrastructure



ProFOLD2's distributed training infrastructure is built around PyTorch's NCCL-backed `DistributedDataParallel` (DDP) with a layered abstraction that decouples device management, process orchestration, model wrapping, and checkpoint persistence. The design targets multi-node GPU clusters managed by SLURM while remaining transparently compatible with single-GPU workflows through a zero-configuration fallback path. This page dissects each layer—from process spawning to gradient synchronization—revealing the mechanisms that make large-scale protein structure model training tractable.

## Architecture Overview

The distributed stack is organized into four cooperating layers, each encapsulated in its own module. The `XPU` class in [accelerator.py](profold2/model/accelerator.py) abstracts device identity and process group lifecycle. The `worker` module in [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py) orchestrates process spawning, per-rank logging, model wrapping, and state serialization. The training loop in [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py) consumes these abstractions to implement gradient accumulation, mixed precision, and checkpoint management. Finally, utility modules ([snapshot.py](profold2/model/snapshot.py), [profiler.py](profold2/model/profiler.py), [utils.py](profold2/model/utils.py)) provide CUDA memory profiling, kernel-level instrumentation, and atomic checkpoint persistence.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Entry["Entry Point"]
        CLI["main.py → trainer.__main__"]
    end

    subgraph Orchestration["worker.main()"]
        CLI --> WL["_WorkerLogging"]
        CLI --> WF["WorkerFunction"]
        CLI --> MP["mp.spawn()"]
        MP -->|rank| WF
    end

    subgraph PerRank["Per-Rank Execution (WorkerFunction.__call__)"]
        WF --> XPU["XPU(rank, nnodes, node_rank)"]
        XPU -->|init_process_group| PG["NCCL ProcessGroup"]
        WF -->|wrap| WM["WorkerModel.wrap()"]
        WM -->|to(device)| GPU["CUDA Device"]
        WM --> DDP["DistributedDataParallel"]
        WF -->|TF32| TF32["torch_allow_tf32(True)"]
        WF -->|cleanup| DPG["destroy_process_group()"]
    end

    subgraph TrainingLoop["train(rank, args)"]
        DDP --> STEP["_step()"]
        STEP --> NSYNC["no_sync_ctx()"]
        STEP --> AMP["accelerator.amp()"]
        STEP --> GS["GradScaler"]
        STEP --> LOSS["loss_scaler = world_size / grad_accum"]
        STEP --> CM["CheckpointManager"]
    end

    subgraph Utilities["Infrastructure Utilities"]
        CM --> CKPT["Checkpoint (atomic save)"]
        CKPT --> SIG["signal-safe rename"]
        PROFILER["profiler.profile()"]
        SNAPSHOT["snapshot.memory_snapshot()"]
    end

    style Entry fill:#1a1a2e,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff
    style Orchestration fill:#16213e,stroke:#0f3460,color:#fff
    style PerRank fill:#0f3460,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff
    style TrainingLoop fill:#533483,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff
    style Utilities fill:#2b2d42,stroke:#e94560,color:#fff
```

Sources: [accelerator.py](profold2/model/accelerator.py#L61-L117), [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L175-L266), [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L75-L468), [utils.py](profold2/model/utils.py#L130-L242)

## Process Orchestration: `worker.main()`

The `worker.main()` function serves as the top-level entry point for all distributed commands. It decides whether to spawn multiple processes (multi-node) or invoke the work function directly (single-GPU), manages logging infrastructure, and coordinates lifecycle hooks. The branching logic hinges on the presence of the `--nnodes` argument: when provided, `mp.spawn()` creates one process per GPU; otherwise, the work function runs in-process with `local_rank` as the device identifier [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L222-L266).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["worker.main(args, fn)"] --> B{"exists(args.nnodes)?"}
    B -->|Yes| C["mp.set_start_method('spawn')"]
    B -->|No| D["Single-GPU path"]
    C --> E["_WorkerLogging(fn, args)"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["work_log.start()"]
    F --> G{"hasattr(fn, 'preprocess')?"}
    G -->|Yes| H["fn.preprocess(args)"]
    G -->|No| I["Skip"]
    H --> J["WorkerFunction(fn, queue)"]
    I --> J
    J --> K{"exists(args.nnodes)?"}
    K -->|Yes| L["mp.spawn(work_fn, nprocs=device_count)"]
    K -->|No| M["work_fn(local_rank, args)"]
    L --> N["work_log.stop()"]
    M --> N

    style A fill:#e94560,color:#fff
    style K fill:#533483,color:#fff
    style L fill:#0f3460,color:#fff
```

Two critical design decisions are worth noting. First, the spawn method is hardcoded to `spawn` rather than `fork`—this is essential for CUDA compatibility, as CUDA contexts cannot be safely forked [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L224). Second, `WorkerLogging` uses a `QueueListener` only in multi-node mode, enabling rank-aware log prefixes while avoiding the overhead of queue-based logging for single-GPU runs [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L75-L80).

### The `WorkerFunction` Per-Rank Wrapper

Once spawned, each rank enters `WorkerFunction.__call__()`, which performs the complete per-rank setup sequence: instantiates an `XPU` with the assigned rank, initializes the log record factory to safely serialize tensors in log messages, attaches a `QueueHandler` with a rank-aware filter, calls `xpu.init_process_group()`, enables TF32 via a context manager, invokes the actual work function, and finally tears down the process group [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L182-L219).

> [!TIP]
> The `torch_allow_tf32(True)` context in `WorkerFunction.__call__` is critical for Ampere+ GPU performance—it allows the hardware's TF32 tensor cores to accelerate matmul and convolution operations, which dominate Evoformer compute [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L213-L214). This can provide up to 2× throughput improvement on A100 GPUs with minimal numerical impact for training workloads.

Sources: [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L222-L266), [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L175-L219)

## Device Abstraction: `XPU` Class

The `XPU` class provides a unified abstraction over CUDA devices with distributed awareness. It encapsulates three identity dimensions—`local_rank` (GPU index within a node), `node_rank` (node index within the cluster), and the computed global `rank`—and manages the NCCL process group lifecycle [accelerator.py](profold2/model/accelerator.py#L61-L117).

| Property/Method | Behavior | Distributed Relevance |
|---|---|---|
| `device` | Returns `local_rank` as CUDA device index; falls back to `torch.device('cpu')` | Determines which GPU this rank binds to |
| `rank` | Computed as `device_count() * node_rank + local_rank`, overridable via `RANK` env var | Unique global identifier across all nodes |
| `is_master()` | True only when `node_rank == 0 and local_rank == 0` | Gates checkpoint saves, TensorBoard writes, and WandB init |
| `world_size()` | `device_count() * nnodes`, overridable via `WORLD_SIZE` env var | Used for loss scaling compensation |
| `init_process_group()` | Initializes NCCL with configurable `timeout` (default 1800s via `NCCL_TIMEOUT`) | The actual distributed backend bootstrap |
| `memory_summary()` | Delegates to `torch.cuda.memory_summary()` | Per-rank GPU memory diagnostics |

The `init_process_group` method hardcodes the `nccl` backend, which is the only viable option for multi-node GPU training in PyTorch. The timeout is configurable via the `NCCL_TIMEOUT` environment variable with a generous default of 1800 seconds, reflecting the reality that protein structure training iterations with large MSA inputs can be exceptionally slow [accelerator.py](profold2/model/accelerator.py#L96-L111).

Sources: [accelerator.py](profold2/model/accelerator.py#L61-L117)

## Model Wrapping and State Management: `WorkerModel`

`WorkerModel` encapsulates all model-level distributed concerns: device placement, DDP wrapping, state dictionary key migration, checkpoint loading, and checkpoint saving. It is instantiated in the training function with the rank-derived `XPU` instance [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L91-L173).

### DDP Wrapping

The `wrap()` method constructs an `AlphaFold2` model, moves it to the assigned CUDA device, and wraps it in `nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel` with three notable configuration choices:

1. **`find_unused_parameters=False`**: All parameters are expected to receive gradients every forward pass. Setting this to `False` avoids the extra communication overhead of an all-reduce to detect unused parameters [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L145).
2. **`_set_static_graph()`**: This optimizes the DDP communication graph by assuming the model's computation graph does not change across iterations. Since the Evoformer architecture has a fixed topology (conditioned only on input dimensions), this is a safe and valuable optimization that reduces redundant bucket reconstruction [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L147).
3. **`device_ids` and `output_device`**: Both are set to `xpu.device` (the local rank), ensuring correct device binding within each process [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L143-L144).

### State Dictionary Key Migration

The `hook()` method registers a `load_state_dict_pre_hook` that performs backward-compatible key remapping. Two specific migration patterns are handled [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L107-L113):

| Legacy Key Pattern | New Key Pattern | Component |
|---|---|---|
| `(.*)impl.token_emb.(.*)` | `\1impl.embedder.to_single_emb.\2` | Token embedding |
| `(.*)impl.to_pairwise_repr.(.*)` | `\1impl.embedder.to_pairwise_emb.\2` | Pairwise representation |

This allows loading checkpoints trained under an older naming convention without manual conversion.

### Checkpoint Serialization

The `save()` and `load()` methods handle the asymmetry between DDP-wrapped and bare models. On save, the DDP wrapper is unwrapped via `model.module` before serializing the state dict. On load, a bare `AlphaFold2` is reconstructed from the checkpoint config, the key migration hook is registered, and the state dict is applied. The serialized format includes both the model state dict and the full model configuration for reproducibility [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L153-L173).

Sources: [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L91-L173)

## Gradient Accumulation and Communication Control

ProFOLD2's training loop implements gradient accumulation with selective gradient synchronization, controlled via the `no_sync_ctx` context manager and a carefully computed `loss_scaler` [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L60-L66).

### The `no_sync_ctx` Mechanism

The `no_sync_ctx` function conditionally wraps a code block in `module.no_sync()`, which prevents DDP from performing gradient all-reduce on every backward pass. The synchronization is deferred until the final accumulation step, where gradients from all micro-batches are reduced in a single all-reduce operation. This dramatically reduces communication volume—from `gradient_accumulate_every` all-reduces to just one per optimizer step [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L60-L66).

The condition for skipping synchronization is: `it != global_step and jt + 1 != args.gradient_accumulate_every`. This means the very first training iteration after a checkpoint restore also skips `no_sync` (since `it == global_step`), ensuring that the first gradient accumulation window is fully synchronized—a correctness safeguard for the transition from checkpoint to training [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L357-L359).

### Loss Scaling for Distributed Training

The `loss_scaler` compensates for the gradient averaging behavior of DDP across multiple nodes. When DDP averages gradients across `M` nodes, each with batch size `N`, the effective gradient is `M` times smaller than training on a single node with batch `M*N` (when loss is summed, not averaged). The formula implemented is [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L330-L331):

```
loss_scaler = world_size(nnodes) / gradient_accumulate_every
```

This effectively scales the loss by the world size (to compensate for DDP gradient averaging) and divides by the accumulation count (since gradients are summed across micro-batches but only reduced once). The actual backward call applies this scaling: `grad_scaler.scale(r.loss * loss_scaler * length_scaler).backward()` [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L368).

An additional `length_scaler` can be optionally enabled via `--train_apply_sqrt_length_scale`, which normalizes loss by the square root of the mean residue count relative to `max_crop_len`. This prevents longer proteins from dominating the gradient signal during variable-length training [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L350-L354).

> [!TIP]
> The gradient accumulation pattern in `_step()` zeroes gradients once at the start, then accumulates over `gradient_accumulate_every` micro-batches with `no_sync` on all but the last step. Combined with the loss scaling formula, this achieves mathematically equivalent training to a single-GPU setup with batch size `world_size × gradient_accumulate_every × per_gpu_batch`—but with drastically reduced communication overhead [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L333-L384).

Sources: [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L60-L66), [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L306-L384)

## Mixed Precision Training

ProFOLD2 integrates PyTorch's AMP (Automatic Mixed Precision) through the `accelerator` module, which provides a unified interface for device-agnostic autocast and gradient scaling [accelerator.py](profold2/model/accelerator.py#L28-L58).

### Autocast Configuration

The `accelerator.amp()` context manager wraps `torch.amp.autocast` with two important customizations. First, the device type is automatically detected via `device_type()`, defaulting to `cuda` when available. Second, the autocast dtype is resolved through `autocast_dtype()`, which follows a priority chain: the `profold2_amp_dtype` environment variable (accepting `float16`, `bfloat16`, or `float32`), then hardware BF16 support detection via `torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported()`, and finally falling back to `float16` [accelerator.py](profold2/model/accelerator.py#L32-L58).

A notable workaround disables `cache_enabled=True` for PyTorch ≥ 1.10.0, as the comment acknowledges this would crash—an unresolved issue likely related to the complex non-standard control flow in the Evoformer's attention patterns [accelerator.py](profold2/model/accelerator.py#L52-L54).

### Gradient Scaling

The `GradScaler` is partially applied with the detected device type and enabled conditionally via `--amp_enabled`. It wraps both the loss backward call and the optimizer step, preventing underflow in float16 gradients while automatically skipping steps with inf/nan gradients [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L329-L383).

| AMP Component | Activation Flag | Config Path |
|---|---|---|
| `autocast` dtype selection | Always active when AMP enabled | `profold2_amp_dtype` env var → BF16 support → FP16 fallback |
| `GradScaler` | `--amp_enabled` | `accelerator.GradScaler(enabled=args.amp_enabled)` |
| TF32 matmul/cudnn | Always enabled in distributed mode | `torch_allow_tf32(True)` in `WorkerFunction` |

Sources: [accelerator.py](profold2/model/accelerator.py#L28-L58), [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L329-L383)

## Checkpoint Management: `CheckpointManager`

The `CheckpointManager` class in [utils.py](profold2/model/utils.py#L130-L242) provides TensorFlow-style periodic checkpointing with automatic rotation, atomic writes, and signal-safe persistence.

### Architecture

The manager wraps a `Checkpoint` object, which stores references to any PyTorch object implementing `state_dict()` (model, optimizer, learning rate schedulers). On `save()`, it serializes all checkpointables to a numbered `.ckpt` file and trims older checkpoints beyond `max_to_keep`. On `restore_or_initialize()`, it finds the numerically largest checkpoint file, restores all checkpointables, and returns the global step as an integer [utils.py](profold2/model/utils.py#L130-L242).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant T as train()
    participant CM as CheckpointManager
    participant CKPT as Checkpoint
    participant FS as Filesystem

    T->>CM: __init__(directory, max_to_keep, model, optimizer)
    CM->>CKPT: Checkpoint(model=model, optimizer=optimizer)
    CM->>FS: mkdir(directory)

    T->>CM: restore_or_initialize()
    CM->>FS: list_checkpoints(directory, sort_numerical)
    alt No checkpoints found
        CM-->>T: return -1
    else Checkpoint exists
        CM->>CKPT: restore(latest.ckpt)
        CKPT->>FS: torch.load(latest.ckpt)
        CKPT-->>CM: success
        CM-->>T: return global_step
    end

    loop Every checkpoint_every steps
        T->>CM: save(global_step)
        CM->>CKPT: save(global_step.ckpt)
        Note over CKPT,FS: Signal-safe atomic write via tmp + rename
        CM->>CM: _trim_checkpoints()
        CM->>FS: unlink(oldest.ckpt)
    end
```

### Atomic Checkpoint Writes

The `Checkpoint.save()` method implements atomic persistence through a two-step protocol: first, the state dict is written to a temporary file with a unique ID (`tmp-{unique_id()}`), then the temporary file is atomically renamed to the target path using `os.rename()` [utils.py](profold2/model/utils.py#L59-L93). On POSIX-compliant filesystems, `rename` is an atomic operation, ensuring that a crash during write never produces a corrupt checkpoint. A `SIGINT` handler is temporarily installed during the write to prevent Ctrl+C from interrupting the serialization [utils.py](profold2/model/utils.py#L68-L73).

### Distributed Checkpoint Behavior

Checkpoint saves are gated by `wm.is_master()`—only the rank-0 process on node-0 writes checkpoint files, preventing race conditions and redundant I/O. On restore, each rank independently loads the same checkpoint file (since `restore_or_initialize()` is called before DDP wrapping is complete in the training function's control flow). The `restore()` method applies `strict=False` for `nn.Module` objects, allowing partial checkpoint restoration when model architectures differ slightly between versions [utils.py](profold2/model/utils.py#L116-L117).

Sources: [utils.py](profold2/model/utils.py#L37-L242), [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L307-L317)

## Distributed Logging Infrastructure

The logging system is designed around the challenge that multiple distributed processes must emit structured, rank-attributed logs to both console and per-rank files without interleaving corruption [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L19-L89).

### Architecture

The `_WorkerLogging` class creates two handlers per worker: a `StreamHandler` for console output and a `FileHandler` for persistent logs named `{work_fn_name}_{node_rank}-{local_rank}.log`. In multi-node mode, a `QueueListener` is initialized with these handlers, and each spawned process attaches a `QueueHandler` that feeds into the central queue [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L56-L89).

The `_WorkerLogFilter` prepends `"Rank {rank} | "` to every message from non-master ranks, making it trivial to trace distributed issues from a single aggregated log file. The `_WorkerLogRecordFactory` pre-processes log arguments to safely serialize PyTorch tensors—converting scalars to `.item()` and multi-dimensional tensors to `.tolist()`—preventing encoding errors when tensors appear in log messages [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L19-L51).

| Component | Single-GPU | Multi-Node |
|---|---|---|
| File handler | `train_0.log` | `train_0-{local_rank}.log` per rank |
| Queue-based logging | Not used (no `QueueListener`) | `QueueListener` + per-rank `QueueHandler` |
| Rank prefix | Not applied | `Rank {global_rank} | ` prepended |
| Tensor serialization | Active | Active |

Sources: [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L19-L89)

## Diagnostics Utilities

Two utility modules provide complementary observability into training: `profiler.py` for compute profiling and `snapshot.py` for CUDA memory debugging.

### Kernel Profiling: `profiler.profile()`

The `profile()` context manager wraps `torch.profiler.profile` with a global `_enabled` flag that also controls `record_function()` annotations scattered throughout the codebase. When enabled, all `record_function(name)` blocks in the Evoformer and structure module become visible in TensorBoard traces, providing kernel-level insight into attention compute, tensor contractions, and communication overhead [profiler.py](profold2/model/profiler.py#L12-L32).

### CUDA Memory Snapshots: `snapshot.memory_snapshot()`

The `memory_snapshot()` context manager leverages PyTorch ≥ 2.1's `torch.cuda.memory._record_memory_history()` API to capture a full memory allocation history during the wrapped code block. On exit, it dumps a pickle snapshot that can be loaded in the PyTorch memory visualizer for identifying allocation patterns, fragmentation, and peak memory sources [snapshot.py](profold2/model/snapshot.py#L15-L56). The snapshot filename auto-generates from hostname, timestamp, and device index, making it safe to collect snapshots from multiple ranks simultaneously without filename collisions.

Both utilities gracefully degrade when their requirements are not met (CUDA unavailable, PyTorch version too old) by logging a warning and passing through as a no-op context [snapshot.py](profold2/model/snapshot.py#L17-L22).

Sources: [profiler.py](profold2/model/profiler.py#L1-L33), [snapshot.py](profold2/model/snapshot.py#L1-L56)

## SLURM Launch Configuration

The [examples/train.job](examples/train.job) file demonstrates the canonical multi-node launch configuration, integrating SLURM scheduling with ProFOLD2's distributed arguments.

### Multi-Node vs. Local Launch Paths

The job script automatically detects the launch environment and configures the distributed arguments accordingly. Under SLURM, the master address is extracted from `SLURM_JOB_NODELIST` via `scontrol show hostnames`, and `srun` is used as the process launcher. Under local mode, `--nnodes` and `--node_rank` are set from environment variables with sensible defaults [examples/train.job](examples/train.job#L47-L63).

| Parameter | SLURM Mode | Local Mode |
|---|---|---|
| `--nnodes` | Inferred from SLURM allocation | `${nnodes:-1}` |
| `--node_rank` | Inferred from SLURM | `${node_rank:-0}` |
| `--init_method` | `tcp://{master_addr}:{master_port}` | `tcp://127.0.0.1:{port}` |
| Process launcher | `srun python` | `python` |
| `NCCL_SOCKET_FAMILY` | `AF_INET` | `AF_INET` |
| `NCCL_TIMEOUT` | `3600` | `3600` |

### Complete Launch Example

The following command launches a 2-node, 4-GPU training job with 24-step gradient accumulation, offline WandB tracking, and a 150M-parameter model configuration:

```bash
# SLURM multi-node launch
srun python main.py \
    --init_method=tcp://${master_addr}:23456 \
    train \
    --prefix=./150m.folding \
    --checkpoint_max_to_keep=10 \
    --num_batches=10000 \
    --batch_size=1 \
    --gradient_accumulate_every=24 \
    --learning_rate=0.0001 \
    --model_evoformer_depth=64 \
    --model_dim 384 256 128 \
    --model_evoformer_accept_msa \
    --wandb_mode=offline

# Local single-node multi-GPU launch
python main.py \
    --nnodes=1 --node_rank=0 \
    --init_method=tcp://127.0.0.1:23456 \
    train --prefix=./output ...
```

Sources: [examples/train.job](examples/train.job#L1-L131), [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L814-L848)

## CLI Reference: Distributed Arguments

The following table summarizes all distributed-specific CLI arguments, defined in the `__main__` block of [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L814-L831) and consumed throughout the worker infrastructure:

| Argument | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--nnodes` | `int` | `None` | Number of nodes. When absent, runs in single-GPU mode |
| `--node_rank` | `int` | `0` | Rank of the current node (0-indexed) |
| `--local_rank` | `int` | `None` | GPU index within the node |
| `--init_method` | `str` | `file:///tmp/profold2.dist` | Process group init URL (file:// or tcp://) |
| `--gradient_accumulate_every` | `int` | `16` | Micro-batches per optimizer step |
| `--amp_enabled` | `flag` | `False` | Enable automatic mixed precision |
| `--checkpoint_every` | `int` | `100` | Save checkpoint every N steps |
| `--checkpoint_max_to_keep` | `int` | `5` | Maximum checkpoint files to retain |
| `--batch_size` | `int` | `1` | Per-GPU batch size (effective batch = `batch_size × world_size × grad_accum`) |

Environment variables that configure distributed behavior without CLI exposure:

| Variable | Used In | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `WORLD_SIZE` | `accelerator.world_size()` | Override world size calculation |
| `RANK` | `XPU.rank` | Override global rank calculation |
| `NCCL_TIMEOUT` | `XPU.init_process_group()` | Process group timeout in seconds |
| `profold2_amp_dtype` | `accelerator.amp()` | Force autocast dtype (f16/bf16/f32) |
| `NCCL_SOCKET_FAMILY` | External (job script) | Set to `AF_INET` for SLURM compatibility |

Sources: [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L674-L686), [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L810-L831), [accelerator.py](profold2/model/accelerator.py#L24-L25)

## Key Design Patterns and Trade-offs

The distributed training infrastructure embodies several deliberate design decisions that balance performance, correctness, and operational simplicity.

**Static graph optimization.** The `_set_static_graph()` call on the DDP wrapper is a significant performance optimization for the Evoformer, which has a deeply nested but structurally invariant computation graph. This avoids the overhead of DDP's automatic bucket rebuilding on every iteration, which can save seconds per step on large models [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L147).

**Master-gated side effects.** Checkpoint saves, TensorBoard writes, WandB initialization, and evaluation all check `wm.is_master()` before executing. This is the simplest correct strategy for operations that should happen exactly once in a distributed run, though it means non-master ranks are idle during these phases [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L199-L201), [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L413-L417).

**Non-distributed data parallelism.** The `dataset.load()` function supports `DistributedSampler` when `num_replicas` and `rank` are provided, but the training loop does not pass these parameters. Instead, each rank runs an independent data loader with identical configuration. This works correctly because each rank uses different random seeds derived from its rank, producing different data ordering. However, it does not guarantee non-overlapping data partitions across ranks—a design choice that prioritizes simplicity over strict data partitioning [dataset.py](profold2/data/dataset.py#L2220-L2224).

**Signal-safe checkpoint persistence.** The atomic rename-based checkpoint writing, combined with SIGINT masking during serialization, ensures that training can be safely interrupted at any point without corrupting the latest checkpoint. This is essential for long-running protein structure training jobs that may be preempted by SLURM [utils.py](profold2/model/utils.py#L67-L93).

Sources: [worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L147), [trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L199-L201), [dataset.py](profold2/data/dataset.py#L2220-L2224), [utils.py](profold2/model/utils.py#L67-L93)

---

**Next steps**: To understand the model architecture that this infrastructure trains, see [AlphaFold2 Core Pipeline](5-alphafold2-core-pipeline). For the data pipeline that feeds the distributed training loop, see [Dataset Loading and Cropping](13-dataset-loading-and-cropping). For the CLI command that invokes this infrastructure, see [CLI Command Reference](21-cli-command-reference).

# Web Interface



The ProFOLD2 web interface is a Flask-based front-end that transforms the protein structure prediction pipeline into an accessible, browser-based service. It provides a complete job lifecycle — from FASTA sequence submission through queued execution to interactive result visualization — backed by MySQL for persistence and a separate CLI task runner that consumes prediction results from a serving endpoint. Understanding this layer is essential for anyone deploying ProFOLD2 as a shared resource or integrating its prediction capabilities into a broader bioinformatics platform.

Sources: [app.py](web/app.py#L1-L13)

## Architecture Overview

The web module follows a classic request-response pattern with an asymmetric processing model: the Flask application handles user interaction and data persistence, while a separate `task.py` CLI worker performs the computationally expensive prediction orchestration against a remote serving endpoint. This decoupling means the web server remains lightweight and responsive even while predictions run for minutes or hours.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Flask Application (web/app.py)"
        Browser["User Browser"]
        Routes["Route Handlers"]
        Form["form.py<br/>Validation"]
        DB["db.py<br/>MySQL"]
        Utils["utils.py<br/>File System"]
        Tpls["Jinja2 Templates"]
    end

    subgraph "Background Worker (web/task.py)"
        Runner["task.py CLI Runner"]
        Serving["Serving Endpoint<br/>profold0://host:port"]
        Relaxer["Amber Relaxer"]
    end

    subgraph "Storage"
        MySQL[("MySQL Database")]
        FS[("File System<br/>$ProFOLD_HOME/serving/")]
    end

    Browser -->|HTTP| Routes
    Routes --> Form
    Routes --> DB
    Routes --> Utils
    Routes --> Tpls
    DB <--> MySQL
    Utils --> FS

    Runner -->|pulls queued jobs| DB
    Runner -->|POST prediction| Serving
    Serving -->|JSON: pdb, headers| Runner
    Runner -->|writes pdb/svg/meta| FS
    Runner -->|updates status| DB
    Runner -.->|optional| Relaxer
```

The serving directory layout produced by the task worker follows a deterministic path structure rooted at `$ProFOLD_HOME/serving/`, with separate subdirectories for logs and per-job data:

```
$ProFOLD_HOME/serving/
├── logs/
│   └── {job_id}.log          # Job-level execution log
└── data/
    └── {job_id}/
        ├── {task_id}.pdb      # Unrelaxed predicted structure
        ├── relaxed_{task_id}.pdb  # Amber-relaxed structure
        ├── {task_id}.svg      # Predicted distance/contact map
        └── {task_id}.log      # Task-level metadata + pLDDT
```

Sources: [utils.py](web/utils.py#L6-L31), [app.py](web/app.py#L9)

## Module Composition

The web interface is composed of five Python modules, each with a clearly defined responsibility within the overall architecture.

| Module | Responsibility | Key Dependencies |
|--------|---------------|-----------------|
| `web/app.py` | Flask application, route definitions, resource serving | Flask, `web.db`, `web.form`, `web.utils` |
| `web/db.py` | MySQL connection management, job/task CRUD operations | `mysql.connector`, `shortuuid`, `parse_fasta` |
| `web/form.py` | Input validation (FASTA, Job ID, email) | `residue_constants`, `parse_fasta` |
| `web/task.py` | Background job execution against serving endpoint | `requests`, `torch`, `matplotlib`, `relaxer` |
| `web/utils.py` | File system path resolution for serving artifacts | `os` |

Sources: [app.py](web/app.py#L1-L13), [db.py](web/db.py#L1-L10), [form.py](web/form.py#L1-L8), [task.py](web/task.py#L1-L27), [utils.py](web/utils.py#L1-L4)

## Database Layer

The persistence layer in `web/db.py` wraps a MySQL database named `profold` with two core tables: `jobs` (submission-level metadata) and `tasks` (individual protein sequences within a job). The connection uses a lazy singleton pattern with automatic reconnection via `ping(reconnect=True)` to handle long-running server deployments.

The `jobs` table tracks the overall submission lifecycle, including the app type, email, raw FASTA input, status, and three timestamps (creation, run start, completion). The `tasks` table stores each parsed protein entry with its own independent status, allowing granular progress tracking for multi-protein submissions.

Sources: [db.py](web/db.py#L14-L42)

### Status Machine

Jobs and tasks progress through four discrete states, each tracked as a `varchar(10)` column:

| Status Constant | String Value | Meaning |
|----------------|-------------|---------|
| `STATUS_QUEUING` | `"Queuing"` | Submitted but not yet picked up by the worker |
| `STATUS_RUNNING` | `"Running"` | Currently being processed |
| `STATUS_DONE` | `"Done"` | Successfully completed |
| `STATUS_ERROR` | `"Error"` | Failed during execution |

These constants are defined at module level and referenced uniformly across `db.py`, `task.py`, and the Jinja2 templates for status-color mapping.

Sources: [db.py](web/db.py#L47-L50)

### Key Database Operations

The `db.py` module exposes a focused set of functions that the rest of the web module depends on. `job_new()` is the entry point for submissions: it generates a short UUID via `shortuuid.uuid()[:10]` (unless a custom Job ID is provided), parses the FASTA string into individual sequences using `parse_fasta()`, and inserts both the job record and its child task records in a single transaction with rollback on failure. `job_get()` retrieves jobs with optional task inclusion and supports flexible querying via `**kwargs` with configurable `logic_op` (`'and'`/`'or'`). The `job_set()` function handles status transitions at both job and task granularity.

> [!TIP]
> The `job_get()` function returns a **single job dict** when called with a `job_id` kwarg using `logic_op='and'` (the default), but returns a **list** for any other query combination. This implicit return-type polymorphism means callers must be aware of the calling convention — the route handlers in `app.py` rely on this behavior consistently.

Sources: [db.py](web/db.py#L56-L179)

### Application Registry

The system supports multiple prediction backends through a simple dictionary registry. Two apps are currently defined:

```python
APP_LIST = {'profold0': 'ProFOLD zero', 'abfold': 'AbFOLD'}
```

The `app_id` is passed via the `?app=` query parameter on every request, defaulting to `'profold0'`. This value determines which app's job queue is displayed in the sidebar status panel and which jobs appear in search results, providing namespace isolation between different prediction services sharing the same database.

Sources: [db.py](web/db.py#L52-L53), [app.py](web/app.py#L18)

## Route Structure and Request Flow

The Flask application defines seven routes that cover the complete user journey. Each route is annotated with its HTTP methods and URL pattern, and most accept an optional `?app=` query parameter for multi-app switching.

### Submission Flow (`/`, `/index/`, `/submit/<job_id>/`)

These three URL patterns all map to the same `submit()` function. On `GET` requests, the form is rendered with optional pre-filled data (when resubmitting via `/submit/<job_id>/`). On `POST` requests, the form data flows through `form.validate()`, and if validation passes, `db.job_new()` persists the submission and redirects to the checking page. The form accepts FASTA sequences either as pasted text (`sequences` field) or as an uploaded file (`sequence_file` field), with file upload taking priority when both are present.

Sources: [app.py](web/app.py#L195-L235), [form.py](web/form.py#L19-L34)

### Checking Page (`/checking/<job_id>/`)

The checking page implements a classic server-polling pattern. It embeds a `<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="30">` tag when the job status is not `"Done"`, causing the browser to automatically reload every 30 seconds. The refresh interval is configurable via the `?refresh=` query parameter. Client-side JavaScript also maintains a countdown timer for the next refresh and persists recently viewed job IDs in `localStorage` for quick switching between jobs.

Sources: [app.py](web/app.py#L33-L53), [checking.html](web/templates/checking.html#L3-L13)

### Result Page (`/result/<job_id>/<task_id>/`)

The result page provides the primary output visualization. It loads the relaxed PDB structure into a **3Dmol.js** viewer for interactive 3D manipulation (cartoon rendering with spectrum coloring), displays the predicted distance matrix as an SVG image, and surfaces the pLDDT confidence metric. JavaScript-based selectors allow switching between tasks within a job and between historical jobs stored in `localStorage`.

Sources: [result.html](web/templates/result.html#L1-L158), [app.py](web/app.py#L56-L68)

### Resource Download (`/resource/<job_id>/<data>/` and `/resource/<job_id>/<task_id>/<data>/`)

The resource endpoint serves prediction artifacts for download. When no `task_id` is specified, it packages all tasks into a single ZIP file containing FASTA, unrelaxed PDB, relaxed PDB, and SVG for each protein. When a `task_id` is given, it supports downloading individual files (`pdb`, `relaxed_pdb`, `svg`) or a per-task ZIP archive. All ZIP generation happens in-memory using `io.BytesIO` to avoid temporary file system clutter.

Sources: [app.py](web/app.py#L71-L137)

### Complete Route Map

| Route | Methods | Purpose |
|-------|---------|---------|
| `/`, `/index/` | GET, POST | Main submission form |
| `/submit/<job_id>/` | GET, POST | Resubmit with pre-filled form |
| `/search/` | POST | Search jobs by ID or email |
| `/checking/<job_id>/` | GET | Poll job status with auto-refresh |
| `/result/<job_id>/<task_id>/` | GET | View prediction results with 3D viewer |
| `/resource/<job_id>/<data>/` | GET | Download job-level or task-level resources |
| `/resource/<job_id>/<task_id>/<data>/` | GET | Download specific task artifact |
| `/diff/<exp_name>/` | GET | Side-by-side experiment comparison |
| `/error/` | GET | Generic error page |

Sources: [app.py](web/app.py#L16-L192)

## Input Validation

The `form.py` module implements thorough input sanitization through the `validate()` function, returning a list of human-readable error strings that the template renders as red list items. The `var_get()` helper function abstracts the dual-source pattern (form field or file upload) used throughout the submission flow, with an optional `func` parameter for post-processing (e.g., `parse_fasta`).

Validation rules are applied in three stages:

1. **Job ID** — Must be 4–20 characters, alphanumeric plus underscore only, and unique across the database.
2. **FASTA sequences** — Parsed via `parse_fasta()`, each sequence must be 1–1024 residues, each description must be under 1024 characters, every residue must exist in `residue_constants.restype_order`, and total input size must be under 64KB.
3. **Email** — Optional, but if provided must match a standard email regex pattern.

When a sequence contains an invalid residue, the error message highlights the offending character in blue with 20 residues of context on each side, making it straightforward for users to locate the problem in long sequences.

Sources: [form.py](web/form.py#L37-L86)

## Background Task Execution

The `task.py` module operates as a standalone CLI tool (invoked via `python web/task.py run`) that bridges the MySQL job queue and a remote prediction serving endpoint. This separation means the web server never blocks on prediction requests — it simply writes jobs to the database, and the worker picks them up asynchronously.

### Task Lifecycle

Each task within a job follows a precise execution sequence orchestrated by `do_task()`. The function POSTs the FASTA string as JSON to the serving URI with a 7200-second (2-hour) timeout. The serving endpoint returns a JSON response keyed by model name, where each result contains a base64-encoded header (PyTorch tensor with confidence scores and distogram logits) and a raw PDB string.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant W as task.py Worker
    participant DB as MySQL
    participant S as Serving Endpoint
    participant FS as File System
    participant R as Amber Relaxer

    W->>DB: job_set(status=Running)
    W->>S: POST JSON {sequence, **params}
    activate S
    S-->>W: 200 JSON {model: {pdb, headers}}
    deactivate S

    W->>W: Decode headers (base64 → torch.load)
    W->>W: Extract pLDDT from confidence.loss
    W->>W: Generate SVG distogram via matplotlib

    W->>FS: Write unrelaxed_{model}_{task_id}.pdb
    W->>FS: Write {model}_{task_id}.svg
    W->>FS: Write {task_id}.log (metadata)

    alt run_relaxer enabled
        W->>R: relaxer.main(pdb_files, output)
        R-->>W: relaxed PDB
        W->>FS: Write relaxed_{model}_{task_id}.pdb
    end

    W->>DB: job_set(status=Done, metrics=JSON)
```

The pLDDT metric is extracted from `header['confidence']['loss']` (a design choice that reuses the loss channel as a per-residue confidence score), and the distogram visualization is generated by taking the argmax of the distogram logits and rendering the resulting matrix as an SVG heatmap. If the serving endpoint returns a non-200 status code, the task is immediately marked as `STATUS_ERROR`.

> [!TIP]
> The URI format uses a custom scheme — e.g., `profold0://127.0.0.1:8080/predictions/profold0_0` — where the scheme identifies the app and the remainder is rewritten to HTTP for the actual request. This convention in `run_jobs()` means the app identifier is embedded in the URI itself, not passed separately.

Sources: [task.py](web/task.py#L39-L151), [task.py](web/task.py#L184-L196)

### Relaxation Integration

When `--run_relaxer` is enabled, each predicted PDB undergoes Amber relaxation after the initial prediction. The relaxer runs in a retry loop (default 2 attempts) to handle transient failures gracefully. If all retry attempts are exhausted, the task is marked as `STATUS_ERROR`. The `--use_gpu_relax` flag controls whether relaxation runs on GPU or CPU.

Sources: [task.py](web/task.py#L115-L142)

### CLI Interface

The task runner supports two subcommands:

```bash
# Run queued jobs (or specific jobs by ID)
python web/task.py run [job_ids...] \
    --uri profold0://127.0.0.1:8080/predictions/profold0_0 \
    --dump_pdb --dump_contact --run_relaxer \
    --use_gpu_relax --relax_retry 2 --skip_task_done

# List/filter jobs from the database
python web/task.py list [--logic_op {and,or}] key=value ...
```

The `run` subcommand can either process all jobs with `STATUS_QUEUING` for the specified app, or target specific job IDs when provided as positional arguments. The `--skip_task_done` flag enables incremental processing, allowing resumed runs after interruption.

Sources: [task.py](web/task.py#L214-L256)

## Template System

The Jinja2 template hierarchy follows a three-level inheritance chain that provides consistent branding and navigation while allowing page-specific content injection.

```mermaid
graph TD
    L["layout.html<br/>HTML skeleton, CSS/JS, navbar, footer"] --> LS["layout-sidebar.html<br/>Content area + sidebar (status panel)"]
    LS --> IDX["index.html<br/>Submission form"]
    LS --> CHK["checking.html<br/>Job status polling"]
    LS --> SRC["search.html<br/>Job search results"]
    L --> RES["result.html<br/>Result visualization (full-width)"]
    L --> DIFF["diff.html<br/>Standalone comparison (no inheritance)"]
    L --> ERR["error.html<br/>Minimal error page"]
```

The base `layout.html` provides the FALCON2 branded navigation bar with a dropdown for switching between registered apps, a global job search input, and includes all CSS (Bootstrap, Font Awesome, custom stylesheets) and JavaScript (jQuery, 3Dmol.js, custom scripts). The `layout-sidebar.html` extends this with a two-column layout: the main content block on the left and a sidebar on the right showing real-time server status (queued/running/done/error counts) and partner logos.

The `diff.html` template is notable for being a standalone page that doesn't inherit from the base layout. It uses Bootstrap 5 loaded from CDN, jQuery from CDN, and 3Dmol.js from cdnjs to render a side-by-side comparison grid of predicted structures versus ground truth, with lazy loading via `IntersectionObserver` to avoid initializing all 3D viewers simultaneously.

Sources: [layout.html](web/templates/layout.html#L1-L152), [layout-sidebar.html](web/templates/layout-sidebar.html#L1-L79), [diff.html](web/templates/diff.html#L1-L100), [error.html](web/templates/error.html#L1-L12)

## Configuration and Deployment

The web server launches on `0.0.0.0:9090` with threading enabled when run directly via `python web/app.py`. The serving module path is controlled by the `ProFOLD_MODULE` environment variable, defaulting to `/serving`, which prefixes all static asset and API URLs in the templates. The data root is determined by `ProFOLD_HOME`, defaulting to the current working directory.

| Environment Variable | Default | Purpose |
|---------------------|---------|---------|
| `ProFOLD_MODULE` | `/serving` | URL prefix for static assets and route mounting |
| `ProFOLD_HOME` | `.` | Base directory for serving data and logs |

The MySQL connection parameters are hardcoded in `db.py` (user: `protein`, password: `folding`, host: `127.0.0.1`, database: `profold`), which means the database must be initialized with these credentials before the web interface can operate. The application does not include automatic database migration — the `jobs` and `tasks` table schemas documented in the module's docstring must be created manually.

Sources: [app.py](web/app.py#L11-L13), [app.py](web/app.py#L238-L240), [utils.py](web/utils.py#L6-L7), [db.py](web/db.py#L56-L72)

## Running the Web Server

To start the web interface in development mode:

```bash
# Set environment variables as needed
export ProFOLD_MODULE=/serving
export ProFOLD_HOME=/path/to/data

# Launch the Flask server
python web/app.py
```

In a production deployment, the web server should be placed behind a reverse proxy (e.g., Nginx) with a WSGI server (e.g., Gunicorn), while the task runner operates as a separate process or cron job:

```bash
# Start the task worker to process queued submissions
python web/task.py run --uri profold0://127.0.0.1:8080/predictions/profold0_0 \
    --run_relaxer --dump_contact -v
```

The two-process architecture means you can scale the web front-end and the prediction worker independently, and the web server remains available even when no predictions are running.

Sources: [app.py](web/app.py#L238-L240), [task.py](web/task.py#L184-L196)

---

For deployment details covering containerized setups, see [Docker Deployment](3-docker-deployment). To understand the prediction serving endpoint that the task worker communicates with, refer to [CLI Command Reference](21-cli-command-reference). For a broader understanding of the prediction pipeline that produces the results visualized in this interface, see [Architecture Overview](4-architecture-overview).

# CLI Command Reference



ProFOLD2 exposes its full capabilities through a unified command-line interface built on Python's `argparse`. The CLI supports three primary subcommands—**train**, **evaluate**, and **predict**—alongside a standalone relaxation tool. Every subcommand rides on a common distributed-execution layer that transparently handles single-GPU, multi-GPU, and multi-node configurations through PyTorch's `mp.spawn` mechanism. This page catalogs every flag, its default value, and the semantics that govern its interaction with the training, evaluation, and prediction pipelines.

Sources: [main.py](main.py#L1-L11), [command/main.py](profold2/command/main.py#L1-L80)

## Entry Point and Invocation Flow

The top-level entry point lives in [main.py](main.py#L7-L11) and delegates to `profold2.command.main.main()`. That function parses arguments, resolves the correct handler function, and passes both into `worker.main()`, which orchestrates distributed process spawning, logging setup, and resource cleanup. The relaxer tool is an exception—it defines its own `argparse` logic and runs independently without the worker infrastructure.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["python main.py \<command\>"] --> B["create_args()"]
    B --> C{"Subcommand?"}
    C -->|train| D["trainer.train"]
    C -->|evaluate| E["evaluator.evaluate"]
    C -->|predict| F["predictor.predict"]
    D --> G["worker.main(args, fn)"]
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H["mp.spawn()"]
    H --> I["fn(rank, args)"]
    
    J["python -m profold2.command.relaxer"] --> K["relaxer.main(args)"]
    K --> L["AmberRelaxation.process()"]

    style A fill:#4A90D9,color:#fff
    style J fill:#4A90D9,color:#fff
    style G fill:#2ECC71,color:#fff
    style K fill:#2ECC71,color:#fff
```

Sources: [command/main.py](profold2/command/main.py#L72-L75), [command/worker.py](profold2/command/worker.py#L222-L265), [command/relaxer.py](profold2/command/relaxer.py#L46-L67)

## Global Arguments

Every subcommand inherits the following top-level flags before its own specialized arguments are parsed. Distributed arguments read from environment variables when not explicitly provided, enabling seamless integration with SLURM and torchrun launchers.

| Flag | Type | Default | Environment Fallback | Description |
|------|------|---------|---------------------|-------------|
| `--nnodes` | `int` | `None` | `SLURM_NNODES` | Number of nodes in the distributed job. When `None`, runs in single-process mode. |
| `--node_rank` | `int` | `0` | `SLURM_NODEID` | Rank of the current node within the job. |
| `--local_rank` | `int` | `0` | `LOCAL_RANK` | Local rank of the accelerator on this node. |
| `--init_method` | `str` | `None` | — | Process group initialization URL (e.g., `tcp://...` or `file:///...`). |
| `-o`, `--prefix` | `str` | `.` | — | Output directory prefix for checkpoints, logs, and results. |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | flag | `False` | — | Enable debug-level logging. |

Sources: [command/main.py](profold2/command/main.py#L19-L62)

> [!TIP]
> When `--nnodes` is set, the worker switches to `mp.spawn` with `start_method='spawn'`. The number of processes spawned equals `accelerator.device_count()` (falling back to 1). Omitting `--nnodes` runs the function directly on the local rank, which is the typical mode for single-GPU inference.

## `train` Command

The training command is the most parameter-rich subcommand. It orchestrates a full training loop with cyclical data loading, gradient accumulation, periodic evaluation, checkpointing, optional tuning steps, and experiment tracking via TensorBoard and Weights & Biases. The function is decorated with a `preprocess` hook that validates model architecture flags and creates the checkpoint directory at [trainer.py#L69-L73](profold2/command/trainer.py#L69-L73).

```bash
python main.py train [global args] [training args]
```

### Data Configuration

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `-t`, `--train_data` | `str` | `train.zip` | Path to the training dataset archive or directory. |
| `--train_idx` | `str` | `None` | Optional index file for the training dataset. |
| `--train_chain` | `str` | `None` | Chain index file for multi-chain training data. |
| `--train_attr` | `str` | `None` | Attribute index file for protein attributes. |
| `--train_data_weights` | `str` | `None` | File containing per-sample weights for weighted sampling. |
| `-n`, `--num_batches` | `int` | `100000` | Total number of training iterations. |
| `-e`, `--eval_data` | `str` | `None` | Evaluation dataset path. When set, periodic eval runs. |
| `--eval_idx` | `str` | `None` | Index file for the eval dataset. |
| `--eval_chain` | `str` | `None` | Chain index for eval data. |
| `--eval_attr` | `str` | `None` | Attribute index for eval data. |
| `--tuning_data` | `str` | `None` | Tuning dataset path (co-trains on a secondary objective). |
| `--tuning_idx` | `str` | `None` | Index file for tuning dataset. |
| `--tuning_chain` | `str` | `None` | Chain index for tuning data. |
| `--tuning_attr` | `str` | `None` | Attribute index for tuning data. |
| `--tuning_data_weights` | `str` | `None` | Per-sample weights for tuning dataset. |
| `--tuning_with_coords` | flag | `False` | Include coordinate labels during tuning steps. |

### Protein and Cropping Filters

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--min_protein_len` | `int` | `50` | Filter out proteins shorter than this. |
| `--max_protein_len` | `int` | `1024` | Filter out proteins longer than this. |
| `--max_msa_size` | `int` | `1024` | Cap the number of MSA sequences per sample. |
| `--max_var_size` | `int` | `8192` | Cap the number of variants per sample. |
| `--num_var_task` | `int` | `1` | Number of tasks within variants. |
| `--min_crop_len` | `int` | `80` | Do not crop proteins shorter than this. |
| `--max_crop_len` | `int` | `255` | Target maximum length after cropping. |
| `--train_apply_sqrt_length_scale` | flag | `False` | Scale loss by √(cropped_length / max_crop_len). |
| `--crop_algorithm` | `str` | `auto` | Cropping strategy: `auto`, `random`, or `knn`. |

### Data Augmentation and Sampling

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--train_crop_probability` | `float` | `0.0` | Probability of cropping a protein during training. |
| `--train_pseudo_linker_prob` | `float` | `0.0` | Probability of loading complex (multi-chain) data with pseudo linkers. |
| `--data_rm_mask_prob` | `float` | `0.0` | Probability of removing masked amino acids. |
| `--train_msa_as_seq_prob` | `float` | `0.0` | Probability of treating an MSA row as the query sequence. |
| `--train_msa_as_seq_topn` | `int` | `None` | Restrict MSA-as-seq to the top-N rows by identity. |
| `--train_msa_as_seq_clustering` | flag | `False` | Sample MSA-as-seq from cluster representatives. |
| `--train_msa_as_seq_min_alr` | `float` | `None` | Minimum alignment length ratio for MSA-as-seq. |
| `--train_msa_as_seq_min_ident` | `float` | `None` | Minimum sequence identity for MSA-as-seq. |
| `--tuning_crop_probability` | `float` | `0.0` | Cropping probability for tuning data. |
| `--tuning_pseudo_linker_prob` | `float` | `0.0` | Pseudo linker probability for tuning data. |
| `--tuning_msa_as_seq_prob` | `float` | `0.0` | MSA-as-seq probability for tuning data. |
| `--tuning_msa_as_seq_topn` | `int` | `None` | Top-N restriction for tuning MSA-as-seq. |
| `--tuning_msa_as_seq_clustering` | flag | `False` | Clustering-based sampling for tuning. |
| `--tuning_msa_as_seq_min_alr` | `float` | `None` | Min ALR for tuning MSA-as-seq. |
| `--tuning_msa_as_seq_min_ident` | `float` | `None` | Min identity for tuning MSA-as-seq. |
| `--random_seed` | `int` | `None` | Global random seed for reproducibility. |

### Training Loop and Checkpointing

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--checkpoint_max_to_keep` | `int` | `5` | Maximum number of checkpoint files to retain. |
| `--checkpoint_every` | `int` | `100` | Save a checkpoint every N iterations. |
| `--tuning_every` | `int` | `10` | Run a tuning step every N iterations. |
| `--eval_every` | `int` | `100` | Run evaluation every N iterations. |
| `--gradient_accumulate_every` | `int` | `16` | Number of micro-batches per optimizer step. |
| `-b`, `--batch_size` | `int` | `1` | Micro-batch size per GPU. |
| `--num_workers` | `int` | `1` | DataLoader worker count. |
| `--prefetch_factor` | `int` | `2` | Batches prefetched per worker. |
| `-l`, `--learning_rate` | `float` | `1e-3` | Base learning rate for Adam optimizer. |

The training loop runs from `global_step` to `num_batches` [trainer.py#L396](profold2/command/trainer.py#L396). Gradient accumulation divides effective batch size by the accumulation count, and the loss scaler accounts for distributed world size to keep gradient magnitudes consistent. Checkpoints restore the global step counter, so training resumes seamlessly after interruption.

### Model Architecture Flags

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--model_features` | `str` | `model_features_main.json` | JSON file defining feature computation. |
| `--model_headers` | `str` | `model_headers_main.json` | JSON file defining prediction heads. |
| `--model_recycles` | `int` | `2` | Number of structure recycling iterations. |
| `--model_recycling_frames` | flag | `False` | Enable frame recycling between recycles. |
| `--model_recycling_pos` | flag | `False` | Enable backbone position recycling. |
| `--model_dim` | `int ×3` | `384 256 128` | Model dimensions (single, pair, trash). |
| `--model_num_tokens` | `int` | 33 | Vocabulary size (residue types with X). |
| `--model_evoformer_depth` | `int` | `1` | Number of Evoformer blocks. |
| `--model_evoformer_head_num` | `int` | `48` | Attention heads in Evoformer. |
| `--model_evoformer_head_dim` | `int` | `32` | Per-head dimension in Evoformer. |
| `--model_shard_size` | `int` | `None` | Shard size for memory-efficient Evoformer computation. |
| `--model_dropout` | `float ×2` | `0.15 0.25` | Dropout rates (single representation, pair representation). |
| `--model_evoformer_accept_msa_attn` | flag | `False` | Enable MSATransformer in Evoformer. |
| `--model_evoformer_accept_frame_attn` | flag | `False` | Enable FrameTransformer in Evoformer. |
| `--model_evoformer_accept_frame_update` | flag | `False` | Enable FrameUpdater in Evoformer. |

At least one of `--model_evoformer_accept_msa_attn` or `--model_evoformer_accept_frame_attn` must be enabled—the preprocess hook asserts this [trainer.py#L70](profold2/command/trainer.py#L70). This ensures the model has a valid attention pathway through the Evoformer. For more on these architectural choices, see [Evoformer and Pairformer Blocks](6-evoformer-and-pairformer-blocks).

### Fine-Grained Parameter Control

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--model_params_requires_grad` | `str` | `None` | Regex pattern; only matching parameters receive gradients. |
| `--model_params_requires_hook` | `str` | `None` | Regex pattern; matching parameters get backward hooks (for W&B logging). |
| `--model_params_optim_option` | `str` | `None` | Per-group optimizer options as URL-encoded string (see note below). |

> [!TIP]
> The `--model_params_optim_option` flag uses a custom URL scheme (`optim://pattern?lr=value&...#regex`) to define parameter groups with individual learning rates. Multiple groups are comma-separated. This is particularly useful for differential learning rates between the Evoformer and structure module heads.

Sources: [command/trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L471-L813), [command/trainer.py](profold2/command/trainer.py#L69-L467)

### Experiment Tracking

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--wandb_enabled` | flag | `False` | Enable Weights & Biases experiment tracking. |
| `--wandb_project` | `str` | `profold2` | W&B project name. |
| `--wandb_dir` | `str` | `None` | Local directory for W&B artifacts. |
| `--wandb_name` | `str` | `None` | Custom W&B run name. |
| `--wandb_mode` | `str` | `online` | W&B mode: `online`, `offline`, or `disabled`. |
| `--amp_enabled` | flag | `False` | Enable automatic mixed precision (AMP). |

When W&B is enabled, the model's feature and header configurations are automatically logged to the run config [trainer.py#L200-L201](profold2/command/trainer.py#L200-L201). TensorBoard logs are written to `{prefix}/runs/eval` by the master rank only [trainer.py#L270-L271](profold2/command/trainer.py#L270-L271).

## `evaluate` Command

The evaluate command loads a saved model checkpoint, runs inference over an evaluation dataset, and reports structural quality metrics. It supports distributed evaluation across multiple nodes with automatic dataset sharding. When the model includes a folding head, it computes TM-scores via Kabsch alignment. For fitness and coevolution heads, it serializes per-sample predictions to pickle files.

```bash
python main.py evaluate [global args] [evaluate args]
```

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--map_location` | `str` | `None` | Device mapping for loading the checkpoint. |
| `--model` | `str` | `model.pth` | Path to the saved model checkpoint. |
| `--eval_data` | `str` | `None` | Evaluation dataset directory or archive. |
| `--eval_idx` | `str` | `None` | Index file for the eval dataset. |
| `--eval_attr` | `str` | `None` | Attribute index for eval data. |
| `--eval_without_pdb` | flag | `False` | Skip loading ground-truth PDB coordinates. |
| `--min_protein_len` | `int` | `0` | Minimum protein length filter (default: no filter). |
| `--max_protein_len` | `int` | `1024` | Maximum protein length filter. |
| `--max_msa_size` | `int` | `1024` | Maximum MSA depth. |
| `--max_var_size` | `int` | `None` | Maximum variant count. |
| `--num_var_task` | `int` | `1` | Variant task count. |
| `--min_crop_len` | `int` | `None` | Minimum crop length. |
| `--max_crop_len` | `int` | `None` | Maximum crop length. |
| `--crop_algorithm` | `str` | `random` | Crop strategy: `random`, `domain`, or `knn`. |
| `--crop_probability` | `float` | `0.0` | Cropping probability. |
| `--pseudo_linker_prob` | `float` | `0.0` | Complex data loading probability. |
| `--msa_as_seq_prob` | `float` | `0.0` | MSA-as-seq augmentation probability. |
| `--msa_as_seq_topn` | `int` | `None` | Top-N restriction for MSA-as-seq. |
| `--msa_as_seq_clustering` | flag | `False` | Cluster-based MSA-as-seq sampling. |
| `--msa_as_seq_min_alr` | `float` | `None` | Min ALR for MSA-as-seq. |
| `-b`, `--batch_size` | `int` | `1` | Batch size for evaluation. |
| `--num_workers` | `int` | `1` | DataLoader workers. |
| `--model_recycles` | `int` | `0` | Recycling iterations (default: 0 for eval speed). |
| `--model_shard_size` | `int` | `None` | Evoformer shard size for memory efficiency. |
| `--amp_enabled` | flag | `False` | Enable AMP for evaluation. |
| `--enable_profiler` | flag | `False` | Enable PyTorch profiler output. |
| `--enable_memory_snapshot` | flag | `False` | Enable CUDA memory snapshot. |

The evaluator writes fitness predictions as pickle files (`{prefix}/{pid}_var.pkl`) containing variant predictions, coevolution parameters, and optionally ground-truth labels [evaluator.py#L133-L134](profold2/command/evaluator.py#L133-L134). When folding heads are present, it reports per-protein and average TM-scores across the evaluation set [evaluator.py#L202-L203](profold2/command/evaluator.py#L202-L203).

Sources: [command/evaluator.py](profold2/command/evaluator.py#L25-L205), [command/evaluator.py](profold2/command/evaluator.py#L206-L323)

## `predict` Command

The predict command is the primary inference interface for structure prediction. It accepts FASTA files (single-sequence or A3M format) or pre-built datasets, runs one or more models on each input, applies Amber relaxation, and produces ranked output structures. This is the command used in production for de novo structure prediction.

```bash
python main.py predict [global args] [predict args]
```

### Input Specification

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `fasta_files` | `str[]` | required | One or more FASTA file paths (positional, supports globs). |
| `--fasta_file_list` | `str` | `None` | Text file listing FASTA paths (one per line). |
| `--fasta_fmt` | `str` | `single` | Format: `single` for single-sequence, `a3m` for MSA input. |
| `--data_dir` | `str` | `None` | Load pre-built dataset instead of FASTA files. |
| `--data_idx` | `str` | `None` | Dataset index file. |
| `--add_pseudo_linker` | flag | `False` | Enable complex/multi-chain prediction. |

### Model Loading

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--models` | `str[]` | required | Model paths in `[NAME=]PATH` format (space-separated). |
| `--model_recycles` | `int` | `0` | Number of recycling iterations. |
| `--model_shard_size` | `int` | `None` | Evoformer shard size. |
| `--max_msa_size` | `int` | `1024` | Maximum MSA depth for A3M input. |

The `--models` flag supports a flexible `[NAME=]PATH` syntax: when no `=` is present, the model name is derived from the filename [predictor.py#L111-L117](profold2/command/predictor.py#L111-L117). Multiple models can be specified to produce an ensemble, with outputs ranked by per-model confidence.

### Inference Options

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--num_workers` | `int` | `1` | DataLoader worker count. |
| `--no_relaxer` | flag | `False` | Skip Amber relaxation entirely. |
| `--no_pth` | flag | `False` | Skip saving the raw prediction `.pth` file. |
| `--no_gpu_relax` | flag | `False` | Force relaxation on CPU. |
| `--amp_enabled` | flag | `False` | Enable AMP during inference. |
| `--enable_profiler` | flag | `False` | Enable PyTorch profiler. |
| `--enable_memory_snapshot` | flag | `False` | Enable CUDA memory snapshot. |

### Output Structure

For each input sequence, the predictor creates a directory at `{prefix}/{fasta_name}/` containing:

| File | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `unrelaxed_{model_name}.pdb` | Raw model output before relaxation. |
| `relaxed_{model_name}.pdb` | Structure after Amber refinement (if enabled). |
| `ranked_{i}.pdb` | Models sorted by confidence (best first). |
| `ranking_debug.json` | Confidence scores and ranking order. |
| `timings.json` | Per-stage timing breakdown. |
| `result_{model_name}.pdb` | Full prediction tensors (unless `--no_pth`). |

The ranking system uses the mean pLDDT confidence score from each model's confidence head [predictor.py#L240](profold2/command/predictor.py#L240). Models are sorted in descending order and the ranked PDBs reflect either relaxed or unrelaxed structures depending on whether relaxation was enabled [predictor.py#L244-L255](profold2/command/predictor.py#L244-L255).

Sources: [command/predictor.py](profold2/command/predictor.py#L29-L360), [command/predictor.py](profold2/command/predictor.py#L131-L296)

## Standalone Relaxer Tool

The relaxer operates outside the main CLI dispatcher as a standalone utility. It reads PDB files, applies Amber energy minimization, and writes relaxed structures to a specified output directory. It invokes the same `AmberRelaxation` class used internally by the predictor but can process arbitrary PDB files from any source.

```bash
python -m profold2.command.relaxer <pdb_files...> [relaxer args]
```

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `pdb_files` | `str[]` | required | PDB file paths (positional, supports globs). |
| `-o`, `--output` | `str` | `.` | Output directory for relaxed PDB files. |
| `--prefix` | `str` | `''` | Filename prefix for output files. |
| `-g`, `--use_gpu_relax` | flag | `False` | Run relaxation on GPU. |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | flag | `False` | Enable debug-level logging. |

The relaxer uses a retry mechanism (2 attempts) to handle transient Amber failures, falling back to the unrelaxed structure if relaxation fails [relaxer.py#L183-L196](profold2/command/relaxer.py#L183-L196). For full details on the Amber relaxation parameters and chemistry, see [Amber Relaxation](18-amber-relaxation).

Sources: [command/relaxer.py](profold2/command/relaxer.py#L1-L68)

## Common Patterns and Examples

### Basic Structure Prediction

```bash
python main.py predict \
  -o ./results \
  protein1.fasta protein2.fasta \
  --models model_1.pth model_2.pth \
  --model_recycles 3 \
  --amp_enabled
```

### Distributed Multi-Node Training

```bash
torchrun --nnodes=4 --nproc_per_node=8 main.py train \
  -o ./training_run \
  -t /data/train.zip \
  -e /data/eval.zip \
  --model_evoformer_accept_msa_attn \
  --model_evoformer_depth 48 \
  --model_recycles 2 \
  --num_batches 500000 \
  --gradient_accumulate_every 8 \
  --learning_rate 1e-3 \
  --checkpoint_every 1000 \
  --wandb_enabled
```

### Evaluation with Profiling

```bash
python main.py evaluate \
  -o ./eval_output \
  --model model.pth \
  --eval_data /data/eval.zip \
  --model_recycles 0 \
  --enable_profiler \
  --enable_memory_snapshot \
  -v
```

### Standalone Relaxation

```bash
python -m profold2.command.relaxer \
  predictions/*.pdb \
  -o ./relaxed \
  -g \
  -v
```

## Performance and Diagnostics Flags

Three diagnostic flags are shared across `predict` and `evaluate` for profiling production workloads:

| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--enable_profiler` | Wraps the inference loop with `torch.profiler.profile()`, emitting a CUDA-time-sorted table at completion. |
| `--enable_memory_snapshot` | Captures CUDA memory snapshots via `snapshot.memory_snapshot()` at each inference step. |
| `--amp_enabled` | Activates `accelerator.amp()` context for automatic mixed precision inference, reducing GPU memory by approximately 30-50%. |

The profiler and memory snapshot can be used simultaneously. When enabled, profiling output is written to debug-level logs and memory summaries are printed at task completion [predictor.py#L293-L295](profold2/command/predictor.py#L293-L295).

For deeper architectural context on how these commands interact with the model components discussed here, proceed to [AlphaFold2 Core Pipeline](5-alphafold2-core-pipeline). For distributed training infrastructure details, see [Distributed Training Infrastructure](19-distributed-training-infrastructure).
